Weekly Project:
The most important thing I learned from this course is that digital thinking is essentially a process: you break something down, convert it into another form, and then reconstruct it. It sounds simple, but this approach has changed the way I view many things.

Before taking this course, I thought digital technology was primarily about computers, software, and code. Now, I realize it represents a much broader way of thinking—it’s not just about using devices, but about deconstructing objects, transforming information, and reassembling the pieces.

Take communication, for example. When we speak, our voices are analog signals—simply vibrations in the air. Yet, technology can capture these sounds, break them down into smaller fragments, convert them into data, transmit them elsewhere, and then reconstruct a new sound for another person to hear. This new sound doesn't need to be physically connected to the original; as long as it contains enough information for us to recognize and understand it, that is sufficient.

This same concept has also given me a new perspective on language. Different languages ​​have vastly different pronunciations, structures, and ways of thinking. However, digital systems can break communication down into smaller units and reassemble them into a different system entirely. The original structure doesn't necessarily have to be preserved; what matters is whether the new structure still holds meaning for someone.

This also explains why entities like HAL 9000 or Miku sound so remarkably human. They aren't merely recordings of human voices; rather, they are the result of human expression being broken down, translated into a different system, and reconstructed through technology. The final product is neither entirely human nor entirely machine.

Muybridge and Marey allowed me to visualize this same process. By capturing sequences of motion and breaking movement down into discrete moments, they made visible things that usually escape our notice. Motion ceased to be a continuous whole and instead became a series of distinct units.

Ultimately, to me, creative technology is not just a set of tools, but a way of seeing the world. A photograph, a sound, a language, a movement, or even an experience—all of these can be deconstructed and reassembled into something entirely new. What truly fascinates me is that technology not only transforms what we create but also alters the way we perceive the world. While different cultures, languages, and historical eras may yield vastly different outcomes, digital systems often employ similar operations: decomposition, transformation, and reconstruction.

This is precisely why creative technology holds such a strong appeal for me. I am not merely interested in using technology to create art; I want to explore how its underlying logic reshapes the ways we see, listen, communicate, and understand reality.
results_discussion:
Examples were given of simulating human speech during a presentation, or how written text can be converted into code for simulation or storage.
In a linguistic context—referencing the prefix "tele-" (meaning "at a distance")—the telegraph was described as representing a form of "digital thinking."
It was noted that most modern communication systems operate by breaking information down into discrete units, transmitting them via satellite to another location, and then reassembling them. Linguistically, this allows for the reconstruction of vastly different languages ​​through total deconstruction; one need not use the original structural modules, but simply break the language down and reassemble it in a way the recipient understands. This explains why HAL 9000 sounds so peculiar when simulating a human voice: our speech and written language were deconstructed and reassembled into a machine-readable format, which the machine then used to synthesize our voices. It is truly fascinating; I now understand why Miku's voice sounds the way it does.
A second example of digital technology involved Eadweard Muybridge. Applying a digital mindset, he set up fixed cameras to photograph racehorses—settling a wager with Stanford University's first president by proving there is a moment when all four of a horse's hooves are off the ground. This illustrates the logic of simulation technology. The work of Étienne-Jules Marey, another observer of animal movement, was also cited as an example.
The latter part of the lecture covered chronophotography and mentioned Chronos, the Greek god of time.
An example of digital thinking was shown: a figure dressed entirely in black, captured by high-speed photography, with their movements rendered as a continuous line.
Cubist works were also displayed; these, too, are products of a digital mindset and express how technology has transformed the way we perceive the world.
The development of visual and audio technologies relies on the same underlying principles—simulation and digitization—establishing these as the foundation of modern video art.
Digital thinking is truly significant and has profoundly influenced a vast array of things.
